cues.text: In the last days of December 1532, thieves broke into the parish church of Marseille-en-Beauvaisis, in northern France, and made off with a silver-gilt ciborium holding a number of consecrated Hosts.
Finding little value in the Hosts themselves once they had the precious vessel, the thieves abandoned them in the town's main street, tucking them beneath a large stone.
On New Year's Day 1533, a resident named Jean Moucque was making his way down the same street through a driving blast of wind and snow.

His attention was caught by something unusual: a single stone lying in the open, exposed to the full force of the storm, that had not gathered a single flake of snow on its surface while everything around it lay buried.
Curious, Moucque lifted the stone and discovered the consecrated Hosts beneath it, completely intact despite having been left exposed to bitter winter weather for several days.
Word of the discovery spread quickly through the town, and what had begun as an ordinary theft became, almost overnight, the foundation of a lasting local devotion.
A chapel — the Chapelle des Saintes-Hosties, still standing today beside the parish church — was raised soon afterward to encourage devotion at the site.
Several healings were subsequently attributed to prayer there, most notably that of a paralyzed priest named Jacques Sauvage, who was reportedly cured completely.
Every year on January 2, a solemn Mass continues to mark the anniversary of the discovery.
The Marseille-en-Beauvaisis account joins a substantial body of medieval and early modern tradition built around Hosts abandoned by thieves.
They were preserved against every natural expectation — in this case, not fire or flood but simple exposure to a winter storm the stone itself seemed mysteriously spared.
Nearly five centuries later, the chapel raised over the site of the discovery still stands, a modest and specific monument to one cold New Year's morning in northern France.
